newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FEATURE-Postman reviled as Argentine "Mafia Daddy".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Postman reviled as Argentine "Mafia Daddy".

text.p: Argentine tycoon Alfredo Yabran's enemies say he is such a powerful mobster he runs a "state within the state," feared even by the president and protected by governments since the military dictatorship.
Even in his own home, the postal mogul has been nicknamed "Mafia Daddy" as a joke by younger members of the Yabran clan.

Yabran says he is "just a postman" and points out that no court has charged him. He has taken out newspaper ads to refute "ridiculous theories ... that put me in the role of Al Capone." But a sensational murder case in which police call Yabran their "only lead" to whoever ordered the killing has confirmed the silver-haired 53-year-old Yabran in the role of -- in his own words -- Argentina's "Public Enemy No. 1."

And after nearly two years with Yabran at the heart of charges of corruption in President Carlos Menem's government -- given credibility by the fact that their originator is the widely respected former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo -- Menem has now lost a cabinet minister to the scandal.

The ruling Peronists' indigant denials of links to Yabran fell flat when Interior Minister Carlos Corach and Justice Minister Elias Jassan had to admit they got phone calls from him -- 100 calls in Jassan's case, forcing him to resign.

Corach called it a "witch-hunt" to distract attention from investigations into the January murder of Jose Luis Cabezas, a photographer for the weekly news magazine Noticias, which had published rare pictures of the notoriously camera-shy tycoon.
YABRAN NAME KEEPS COMING UP IN MURDER PROBE

Cabezas was handcuffed, beaten, shot and burnt at a beach resort where Yabran and half the goverment go on holidays. An ex-policeman was arrested for the killing but Yabran's name keeps coming up in the search for who ordered the murder, and phone calls from the suspected killer were traced to his home.

Menem complains that "Yabran has already been condemned by the media," says "it's no crime to be a suspect" and accuses those who link Yabran to Cabezas of wanting to hurt the Peronists' chances of defending their majority in Congress in October. But opinion polls show most people see Yabran's hand in the murder and when he went to the Casa Rosada government palace this week to complain that his business was being hurt by the allegations he was met by a furious mob.

Goaded by the opposition, drivers honked their horns and pedestrians shouted "Murderer! Murderer!" Protesters joined by journalists wielding their microphones and cameras mobbed Yabran's car and smashed its rear window.

Menem, who denies Yabran is his friend but admits he knows him, condemned the mob and those who organised the protest as "outlaws." But by granting Yabran an audience in the Casa Rosada, his government ran the risk of fuelling suspicions.
"It's like Bill Clinton receiving O.J. Simpson in the middle of his trial," Sen. Graciela Fernandez Meijide of the centre-left Frepaso coalition said.
An memo circulating in one ministry warns that "putting Yabran at the centre of the storm could cost Menemism dear" and suggests Menem is defending him "for fear of his life."

One close associate of Yabran told Reuters the businessman believes he has been framed for Cabezas' murder by the police, for whom he was an obvious fall-guy. "He was already being made out to be the source of all evil in Argentina. But Alfredo is absolutely convinced the rule of law will prevail -- in the end," said the man, asking not to be identified.
VICTIM OF A POWER GAME?

Yabran's friends depict him as the victim of a power game between Menem and the Peronist governor of Buenos Aires Province, Eduardo Duhalde. Once close to Menem but now campaigning to succeed him in 1999, Duhalde runs the province where Cabezas was killed and has openly challenged Yabran.

"Some powerful or important people think they deserve special treatment, but they are all equal before the law," Duhalde said last week after Yabran tried to sue him. "I am not against Yabran, I am in favour of the truth."

Yabran has become a ubiquitous bogeyman in this murky world, where nobody is sure which companies he owns but many believe he controls strategic areas like the distribution of official documents and bonded warehouses at the airports. Frepaso coalition chief Carlos Alvarez said Yabran has "built up power in the shadows in sensitive and strategic areas and constructed almost a state within the state."

"Yabran seems to symbolise evil in Argentina now," political analyst James Neilson said. "The strangest thing is that this figure should emerge so suddenly from the darkness and be accused of so many things -- so plausibly."

Congress has set up an Anti-Mafia Commission, originally called the "Anti-Yabran Commission," to probe charges that Yabran used violence to build up his business empire. Former state post office chief Abel Cuchetti says Yabran was behind a beating he suffered and a bomb at his home in 1992, just after a Yabran firm failed to win a postal contract.

Independent Congresswoman Patricia Bullrich says Yabran's rise to riches began during the military dictatorship in the late 1970s. Yabran admits to a fortune of $400 million and one or two firms, but Bullrich puts it closer to $2 billion and says many more firms are in the names of family or friends.

She says letting Yabran into the Casa Rosada "is like Clinton receiving Al Capone in the White House," adding: "If he disappears, we can put an end to a political structure where power, drugs and influence-peddling are all mixed up."
